title: Safety
intro: Your home is a fortress for your cat. Make sure every corner of it is safe and comfortable.

sections.heading: Window screens
sections.body:
Ordinary mosquito screens won't hold up against a cat's jump or claws. And open windows can lead to a cat getting stuck or falling out.

There are two main types of screens for protecting cats:
1) "Anti-cat screens" — made from high-strength steel mesh and securely attached to the frame with metal fasteners around the entire perimeter.
2) Plastic restrictors for open window gaps — also known as "tilt-and-turn window guards."

sections.heading: Protecting corners and gaps
Electricity
Heavy furniture
Household chemicals
Balcony
sections.body:
Being able to enjoy fresh air is an important part of an animal's life. But besides fresh air and sunshine, a balcony can also hide danger.

The first and most important rule is having dedicated safety netting around the entire perimeter of the balcony. You should also seal off any technical openings — cats are curious and will poke their noses in anywhere they can.

sections.heading: Additional points
sections.body:
Kitchen: a hot stovetop; knives; an open oven; the trash can.

Bathroom: keep the toilet lid closed; always check the washing machine before starting it; keep cabinets closed; store pills and capsules securely.

Candles and fragrances: essential oils; diffusers; incense; candles.

Bags and film: plastic bags; packaging film; stretch wrap.

Thread and elastics: sewing thread; embroidery floss; rubber bands; hair ties.

title: Food and water
intro: Create the ideal feeding space for your cat by following the principles of comfort and natural needs.

sections.heading: 1. Choosing bowls
sections.body: Material matters. Plastic accumulates bacteria and can cause feline acne. Recommended materials: glass, ceramic, and stainless steel.

sections.heading: 2. The ideal location
3. A comfortable height
sections.body: Bowls on a stand reduce strain on the neck and joints, especially in older cats. Tilting the bowl to the correct 15-degree angle makes swallowing more natural. Choose the height based on how tall your cat is while standing.

sections.heading: Tip: bowl dimensions
sections.body:
Bowl width: the inner diameter should be at least 1.5–2 times the width of the cat's face (including whiskers). For most adult cats, the optimal diameter is 15–18 cm; for large breeds (such as Maine Coons), 18–22 cm. If the diameter is under 12–13 cm, the cat's whiskers will keep brushing against the sides.

Bowl depth: 2–4 cm is ideal for both dry and wet food. The rim height should be about 1/2–3/4 of the height of the cat's face. Rims taller than 5–6 cm are only suitable for large food volumes and are less convenient for everyday feeding.

title: Heat and cold
intro: How to protect your pet from overheating and hypothermia.

sections.heading: Summer heat
sections.body:
• Always keep a bowl of fresh water within reach. Cats drink more when they're hot.
• Use cooling mats or damp towels, but don't force your cat to lie on them.
• Avoid direct drafts from the air conditioner — ideally, the cool air should not blow directly on the cat. Clean the AC filters as needed.
Don't: don't pour ice water on your cat; don't apply ice directly to its body; don't force it to drink.

sections.heading: Heatstroke risk!
sections.body:
Watch for: rapid open-mouthed breathing; severe lethargy; bright red gums; refusal to eat or drink; loss of coordination.
If these symptoms appear, urgent veterinary care may be needed.

sections.heading: Winter
sections.body:
Cozy beds off the floor, plus humidifying dry indoor air. Create warm spots around the house: bedding and a draft-free location will help retain warmth.

In winter it's important to: avoid drafts; not place the bed near a cold window; maintain 40–60% humidity; and wipe your cat's paws after walks (if it goes outside).

sections.heading: Hidden dangers
sections.body: Hot radiators — prolonged contact can cause burns. Tilted-open windows — a risk of hypothermia and injury.

sections.heading: Something to keep in mind
sections.body: Cats choose their own comfortable temperature. If your pet keeps lying on the cold floor, hiding under a blanket, or staying by the radiator, that's a sign it's too hot or too cold for it.

title: Play
intro: For an indoor cat, play isn't just entertainment — it's an outlet for the hunting instinct. Daily 15–30 minute sessions help prevent stress, obesity, and destructive behavior.

sections.heading: Safety first: choosing materials
sections.body:
Material matters for toys. Cats play with their paws, but they also take toys into their mouths.

Natural materials: wool, feathers, cotton and linen, jute and sisal, wood.
Synthetic materials: fleece, food-grade silicone, quality ABS plastic.

Avoid cheap plastic with a strong smell (it breaks quickly, has sharp edges, and smells toxic), long fibers and tinsel (threads tear off easily and can cause intestinal blockage if swallowed), and foam rubber (a cat can chew through it, and small pieces get stuck in the stomach).

Small parts: no beads, glued-on eyes, or buttons — a cat can easily bite them off and swallow them, leading to serious gastrointestinal injury.

sections.heading: General toy list
sections.body:
Textile and wool: a soft squeaky toy made of cotton/linen; felted balls of 100% wool; fabric mice and fish with no glued-on parts; catnip pouches; plush fleece pillow toys.

Wood and natural fibers: matatabi (silvervine) chew sticks; pressed catnip balls; wooden puzzle mazes; sisal/jute rope balls; scratching posts and mats.

Silicone and rubber: food-grade silicone chew toys; dental massage toothbrush toys; rings made of durable rubber.

Plastic interactive toys (ABS plastic only): multi-level ball-track towers; interactive puzzle feeders; treat-dispensing wobble toys; enclosed plastic balls with a bell.

Toys for play together: wand teasers with fleece ribbons or natural feathers; long textile snake-like cords.

sections.heading: Self-entertainment
sections.body:
Puzzle toys and maze feeders keep your cat occupied while you're away. The best motivation is a favorite dry treat.

Examples: puzzle feeders with lids the cat slides open with its paw; the Catit Senses Food Tree; Nina Ottosson puzzle toys of various difficulty levels; interactive treat balls; snuffle mats; peekaboo puzzle boxes.

sections.heading: Caution
sections.body:
Laser pointers: these can cause frustration, since the "prey" can never actually be caught. Always end the game with a real toy the cat can grip and squeeze with its paws.

Ribbons: never leave a cat unsupervised with ribbons or string — there's a risk of choking or swallowing the thread. It's best to keep these stored in closed boxes the cat can't access.

sections.heading: The golden rule: supervision
sections.body: No toy is 100% safe. Regularly check your cat's toy collection for wear, torn-off parts, or tears. Your attention is the best guarantee of safety.

title: The litter box
intro: Choosing the right litter box and litter has a direct effect on whether your cat will use the bathroom where it's supposed to.

sections.heading: Choosing a litter box
sections.body:
Open type ("classic") — maximum visibility for the cat, ideal for kittens and older cats. Choose sides 15–20 cm high, with a box length of 1.5–2 times the cat's body length.

Covered box ("privacy") — hides odors and litter, and prevents scatter. Some cats may feel trapped inside — try removing the door at first.

sections.heading: Where to place the litter box
sections.body:
A quiet spot — away from noisy appliances and busy hallways.
Away from food — cats don't like relieving themselves where they eat or drink.

sections.heading: Types of litter
sections.body:
Clumping mineral (bentonite clay) — holds odor very well and forms firm clumps, but produces dust when poured.

Wood-based (pressed sawdust, absorbent) — budget-friendly, breaks down into crumbs when wet, can be flushed down the toilet in small amounts, and is eco-friendly.

Silica gel (absorbent) — maximum absorbency and odor control, but crunches loudly and may scare off timid cats.

Plant-based litters (soy, corn, wheat) — flush perfectly, dissolve without residue, are safe if accidentally eaten, but cost more and can attract rodents if stored at a country house.

Wood-based (pressed sawdust, absorbent) — budget-friendly, breaks down into crumbs when wet, can be flushed down the toilet in small amounts, and is eco-friendly.
Silica gel (absorbent) — maximum absorbency and odor control, but crunches loudly and may scare off timid cats.
Plant-based litters (soy, corn, wheat) — flush perfectly, dissolve without residue, are safe if accidentally eaten, but cost more and can attract rodents if stored at a country house.

sections.heading: The golden rule of litter boxes: N + 1
sections.body: You should have one more litter box than you have cats in the house. This helps prevent stress and territorial conflicts.

sections.heading: Care and hygiene
sections.body:
Daily: scoop clumps and solid waste 1–2 times a day.
Every 2 weeks/month: fully replace the litter and wash the box with a mild cleaner.

Material matters: plastic is more affordable, but absorbs odors over time and its chips and scratches can harbor bacteria. Ceramic or metal boxes disinfect more hygienically but cost more.

sections.heading: Hidden threats
sections.body:
Fragrances: a lavender scent may be pleasant to you, but it repels a cat's sensitive nose.
Noisy locations: a litter box next to the washing machine is a recipe for sudden fright and the cat refusing to use that spot.

sections.heading: If your cat ignores the litter box
sections.body:
Medical: first rule out cystitis or urinary stones with a vet.
Behavioral: check cleanliness, and try changing the litter type or the box's location.

Cats may ignore the litter box due to stress, unsuitable litter, a strong odor, or being frightened by the sounds and feel of certain litter particles.

title: Grooming and care
intro: Regular care helps you catch changes in your cat's health early. Most routines take just a few minutes, but it's more important to do them calmly and consistently.

sections.heading: What to check at home
Daily / periodic care
sections.body:
Daily: fresh water; normal appetite; a clean litter box; a quick health check; activity and play.

Periodic: brushing; nail checks; teeth cleaning; ear and eye checks; weight monitoring.

sections.heading: Important
sections.body: Home care doesn't replace a veterinary exam. A new lump, prolonged lethargy, refusal to eat, a sudden change in behavior, constant scratching, or other unusual symptoms are all reasons to see a vet.

sections.heading: Nail trimming
sections.body:
Cats usually don't need their claws shortened by much. The main goal is just to remove the sharp tip, without touching the quick (the living part of the claw).

How to prepare: cat nail clippers; good lighting; a calm location; a treat for after the procedure.

How to trim: 1) let the cat get used to having its paws touched calmly; 2) gently press the paw pad so the claw extends; 3) find the light/pink inner part of the claw; 4) trim only the clear, sharp tip (a couple of millimeters); 5) if the cat gets anxious, do one or two paws and continue later.

How often: check the claws regularly — frequency depends on age, activity level, and whether the cat uses a scratching post. If you accidentally cut into the quick, there may be bleeding and pain — use a styptic product made for animals, and don't force the procedure to continue. Scratching posts remain an important part of a cat's natural claw care and behavior.

sections.heading: Brushing
sections.body:
Brushing helps remove loose fur and reduces the amount of hair a cat swallows while grooming itself.

Benefits: less shed hair around the house; fewer mats; easier to monitor skin condition; easier to spot parasites, irritation, and wounds; especially useful for long-haired cats.

How to choose a tool: short coat — a soft brush or rubber grooming glove; medium coat — a brush with appropriately spaced teeth and a comb; long coat — a comb and brush that can gently work through the fur down to the roots.

title: Free roaming outdoors
intro: Letting a cat roam freely outside may seem "natural," but the modern urban environment hides deadly dangers. Statistically, indoor cats with proper care live 15–20 years, while cats living outdoors live only 4–5 years.

sections.heading: Main risks
sections.body:
Traffic and poisoning by malicious people are the most common causes of death for cats in cities.

Predators and dogs: stray packs and wild animals pose a threat.
Infections: feline leukemia, immunodeficiency virus, and rabies can be transmitted by animals the cat might catch and eat.
Cruelty from people: poisoners, dog-hunters, and simply ill-wishers can harm a defenseless, trusting animal.

sections.heading: Alternatives to free roaming: leash walks
sections.body:
Safe exploration of the world under your supervision. Not every cat enjoys walking on a leash, but with the right preparation, it can be a great source of variety in a cat's days.

Important during walks: make sure vaccinations are up to date; don't let the cat eat anything or interact with anyone outside — it should only eat from your hands or from home.

sections.heading: Catio (outdoor enclosure)
sections.body:
A mesh-enclosed extension that lets your cat breathe fresh air. If you have a private house, you can build a separate cat enclosure. The main goal of such structures is to create a safe outdoor space.

These enclosures are usually built from solid wood and mesh. If dangerous animals may be nearby, use reinforced mesh and anti-digging measures.

title: Flowers and plants
intro: Cats love exploring plants, but some are toxic and life-threatening. This guide will help you choose safe plants and protect your pet.

sections.heading: List of dangerous flowers
sections.body:
Lilies and daylilies — especially dangerous, can cause severe kidney damage.
Dieffenbachia — irritation and swelling of the mouth and throat.
Philodendron — irritation of mucous membranes, drooling, difficulty swallowing.
Monstera — contains insoluble calcium oxalates, causes burning and swelling in the mouth.
Caladium — mouth irritation, swelling of the tongue and lips.
Peace lily (Spathiphyllum) — irritation of mucous membranes and drooling.
Snake plant (Sansevieria) — can cause vomiting and diarrhea.
Ivy — possible vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.
Sago palm (Cycas) — extremely toxic, can cause severe liver damage.
Azalea and rhododendron — vomiting, weakness, heart rhythm disturbances.
Oleander — highly toxic, capable of causing severe heart problems.
Tulips — the bulbs are especially dangerous, causing vomiting and GI irritation.
Daffodils — the bulbs are toxic, causing vomiting, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms.
Hyacinths — the bulbs cause GI irritation.
Chrysanthemums — drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of coordination.
Kalanchoe — toxic to heart function.
Aloe vera — vomiting, diarrhea, and lethargy.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.body: Prevention is the key to safety. If you're not sure whether a plant is safe for your cat, it's best to place it somewhere your pet can't reach. When in doubt, choose a different plant.

sections.heading: What to do in case of poisoning
sections.body:
1. Don't panic, and isolate the cat — remove any remaining plant from its mouth if possible, and don't let it eat anything else.
2. Take a photo of the plant — the vet needs to know exactly which toxin caused the poisoning in order to choose the right antidote.
3. Go to the clinic immediately — don't try to induce vomiting yourself without a vet's instruction. Every minute can count.

title: Activity
intro: Movement is the key to your cat's health and longevity. Create a space for an active life.

sections.heading: Daily exercise
sections.body:
Regular play sessions (15–30 minutes a day) help prevent obesity and maintain muscle tone. Use wand toys and laser pointers to mimic hunting.

Benefits: reduces stress; decreases nighttime activity; prevents destructive behavior; helps control weight; satisfies the hunting instinct.

sections.heading: Vertical routes
sections.body:
Using cat trees and wall-mounted steps lets a cat act on its climbing instinct and feel safe up high.

What this includes: scratching posts at least 80 cm tall; wall shelves; cat trees; window hammocks; bridges.

sections.heading: How to tell your cat needs more playtime
The play process
sections.body:
The general cycle: hunt → catch → eat → rest. In other words: play, then give a small treat or portion of food, then let the cat rest. This cycle closely mirrors natural behavior.

1. Searching for prey — move the toy slowly, hide it behind furniture, and let the cat watch and "stalk" it.
2. The chase — vary the speed and direction, mimic the behavior of a bird or mouse, and let the cat sneak up.
3. The catch — don't keep pulling the toy away constantly; let the cat successfully catch the "prey" several times, and allow it to hold and bite it.

How to tell your cat has had enough: it rests calmly after play; it doesn't demand constant attention; it maintains a normal weight; it damages furniture less; it shows interest in its toys.

sections.heading: Exercise wheel
sections.body:
Helps an indoor cat burn energy, especially if it lives in an apartment without free access to the outdoors. A good addition to playtime, but not a replacement for interaction with you.

Benefits: reduces the risk of obesity; keeps muscles and joints in good condition; reduces boredom and stress; useful for active breeds (Bengal, Abyssinian, Oriental, Savannah).

Good to know: not every cat starts using the wheel right away — some need several weeks to get used to it; never force a cat to run; encourage interest with treats; the wheel should turn smoothly and nearly silently.

sections.heading: Mental stimulation
sections.body:
Puzzle feeders and interactive toys make a cat "work" for its food, which mimics natural behavior and prevents boredom.

Examples: jars with sliding lids; treat-dispensing balls; treat mazes; boxes with holes; snuffle mats.

sections.heading: Tips
sections.body:
"Rotate your cat's toys every week. Novelty is the best stimulus for feline curiosity."
Two short 10–15 minute play sessions are better than one long one — this way the cat doesn't get tired too soon and stays interested.

title: Your workspace
intro: Setting up a cat-friendly home office requires balancing your comfort with your pet's safety.

sections.heading: 01. Dividing the space
sections.body:
Cats like to be at the center of things. Instead of constantly shooing them off the desk, give them their own designated spot: a spot by the window (perfect for bird-watching) or a second shelf on a unit next to the desk for the cat to rest on.

A good option is a bracket-mounted shelf that attaches to the desktop and can swivel in different directions — the cat stays close by without getting in the way of your workspace.

sections.heading: 02. Organizing cables
sections.body:
Cable boxes — hide power strips inside dedicated boxes to keep the cat away from outlets.
Cable conduits — use rigid tubing for cords the cat tends to chew on (chargers, monitor cables).

sections.heading: 03. Keyboard protection
sections.body:
The infamous "walk across the keyboard" can lead to accidentally deleted files or odd messages sent to coworkers.

Use a clear acrylic bridge stand over the keyboard, or set up a "decoy keyboard" — an old keyboard placed nearby can draw your cat's attention away.

sections.heading: 04. Ergonomics and height
sections.body:
Choose furniture with both your pet's jumping habits and your own health in mind.

An adjustable-height desk (recommended): lets you quickly raise the work surface if the cat gets too insistent. Important: keep in mind that when adjusting the desk's height, the moving mechanism and gaps between panels can pinch the cat.

Chair stability (important): a five-point base with locking wheels will prevent tipping if the cat suddenly jumps onto the backrest, or if it's napping under the chair's wheels.

sections.heading: Caution: not recommended

title: Hazards around the home
intro: Your home is a fortress, but for a curious cat it's full of hidden traps. Learn how to prevent tragedy.

sections.heading: Tilt-open windows
sections.body:
A tilted-open window is a deadly trap. Cats try to squeeze out, slip into the narrow gap, and get stuck, which can lead to suffocation, tissue necrosis, or spinal injury.

The solution: side safety grilles or "anti-cat" window systems (not mosquito screens).

sections.heading: Small objects
sections.body: Hair ties, needles, and thread can look like a new toy to a cat. The hunting instinct in these cases can lead to injuries to the paws or internal organs. A swallowed thread can bunch up the intestines like an accordion.

sections.heading: Risk zone: the kitchen
sections.body: Hot stovetops, open dishwashers, and washing machine drums — cats look there for warmth or a hiding spot. It's important that the stove can't turn on just because a cat climbed on it. The best options are mechanical knobs or a lock on the touch panel.

sections.heading: Toxic substances
sections.body:
Many everyday household items are safe for people but can be dangerous or even fatally toxic to cats, even in small amounts.

Household chemicals: floor cleaners, bleach, plumbing/drain cleaners, oven cleaners, laundry pods.
Essential oils: tea tree, eucalyptus, peppermint, citrus, cinnamon, clove.
Medications: acetaminophen, ibuprofen, antidepressants, iron-containing vitamins, cold remedies. Never give a cat human medication without a veterinarian's guidance.

sections.heading: Risk zone: beds
sections.body:
Dangerous materials: choose beds made of safe fabrics and fillings, avoid materials with a strong chemical smell, and check that the fabric doesn't shed or leave loose fibers.

Risk of swallowing parts: avoid beds with sewn-on beads, buttons, or decorative cords; regularly check toys and beds for damage.

Structural stability: securely anchor wall-mounted shelves, and replace any item at the first signs of tearing.

Overheating risk: don't place beds near heaters or radiators.

Cleanliness and allergens: regularly wash removable covers, and use materials that are easy to clean.

title: Your pet's diet
intro: A guide to proper nutrition in a compact format.

sections.heading: Quick rules for good food
sections.body:
Pros: meat as the first ingredient; taurine present; vitamins and minerals.

Cons: sugar and sweeteners; artificial colors; vague "by-products" listed without specifics.

sections.heading: Dry or wet food
sections.body:
Dry food — convenient to store and portion, can be left in the bowl longer, more economical, works well with automatic feeders. Downsides: low moisture content (about 8–10%), requires constant access to water.

Wet food — contains 70–85% water, helps maintain water balance, more appealing to cats that don't drink much. Downsides: more expensive, spoils quickly once opened, can't be left in the bowl for long.

Combined feeding: for example, wet food in the morning, a small portion of dry food midday, and wet food again in the evening.

sections.heading: Choosing food by ingredients
sections.body:
Focus on nutritional completeness and how trustworthy the information is. The label should state that the food is complete and balanced, and suitable for your cat's specific age and condition.

Check the guaranteed analysis (minimum % crude protein and fat, maximum % fiber and moisture). AAFCO standards recommend at least 26% crude protein in dry food for adult cats and 30% for kittens.

Protein: cats are obligate carnivores, so the base of the food should be meat or fish. The first items in the ingredient list should be specific ingredients ("chicken," "turkey," "salmon"), not vague terms like "meat and by-products." Taurine must be present.

Fats: animal sources are preferable (chicken fat, fish oil, salmon oil) — a source of omega-3 and omega-6.

Carbohydrates and fiber: cats don't need many carbohydrates, so corn/wheat/rice aren't ideal as a base ingredient. Fiber is beneficial in moderate amounts (around 3–6%).

Additives: natural preservatives are preferable (vitamin E, vitamin C, rosemary extract) — avoid BHA, BHT, and ethoxyquin.

Risks of low-quality food: allergies, digestive issues, obesity, nutrient deficiencies.

sections.heading: Marketing buzzwords: don't be fooled
sections.body: Labels like "Premium," "Super-premium," "Holistic," "GMO-free," and "Natural" are used often and mean very little — focus on the actual ingredient list and guaranteed analysis rather than marketing labels.

sections.heading: Checklist for choosing food

title: Sleep and rest: creating the perfect spot
intro: How you organize your space has a direct effect on your pet's physical and mental health.

sections.heading: General rule: quiet retreats
sections.body: Every cat should have a place where nothing will disturb it: boxes, tunnels, or fleece cocoons.

sections.heading: A variety of surfaces
sections.body:
Cats appreciate having options — from soft plush beds to simple cardboard boxes, each spot serving its own purpose at different times of day. Watch to see what your particular cat prefers.

Options: soft beds, boxes, shelves.

sections.heading: Vertical space
sections.body:
High vantage points let cats keep an eye on their territory, which reduces stress and anxiety. It's important that there are several ways to get to and from this area.

Minimalist wall shelves; multi-level cat activity towers.

sections.heading: Harmony in a multi-cat household
sections.body: In a home with multiple pets, the formula for ideal rest is simple: N + 1. The number of beds should exceed the number of cats by one, to avoid competition over resources. And more — spread across different spots — is even better.

sections.heading: Types of beds
sections.body:
Enclosed cave beds — ideal for cats that prefer to hide away while resting.
Beds with raised edges — soft baskets with high sides, ideal for cats that like to curl up into a ball while sleeping.
Hammocks — hanging setups mounted to radiators, chair legs, or windows; a favorite spot for active pets that prefer resting up high.
Mats and pads — flat, portable bedding, suited to larger cats or ones that like to sleep stretched out.
Cushion beds — square or rectangular soft options for everyday use.
